There are roughly two ways to make an agent better. You can improve the model —
pretraining, RL, post-training of every flavor — or you can improve the
*program* wrapped around it: the prompts, the workflow, the tools, the
scaffold. Call them parameter space and program space. Parameter space is where
the headline gains come from, but it is closed territory: a point of lift costs
a training run, and a handful of labs can pay. Program space is the opposite —
open to anyone, priced in tens of dollars, iterable in an afternoon — and the
same model routinely swings by double digits depending on the harness it runs
inside.<!-- TODO: pin a real number here — SWE-bench leaderboard spread for a
fixed model across scaffolds is the obvious citation -->

![The two axes. Progress so far has climbed the parameter wall — a training
run per step, flattening returns. The program-space direction is open,
cheap, and — as of roughly now — searchable by machine.](figures/two_axes.png){#fig-two-axes width=88%}

Until recently, program space was searched by hand, which is to say barely:
harness design is a high-dimensional, gradient-free search problem, and humans
explore it by folklore. What changed is that frontier models became good enough
to do the searching — to read an agent's trajectory, diagnose the failure, and
propose an edit. A field has formed around this almost overnight: prompt
evolvers like GEPA [@gepa], workflow searchers like AFlow [@aflow], and the
recursive-self-improvement line — ADAS, the Darwin Gödel Machine — where the
agent rewrites its own scaffold. A new optimizer every few weeks. And if your instinct is that
the next model release makes all of this moot — note that the argument cuts the
other way. The optimizer is a model too. Every release upgrades the thing that
improves the agent, not just the agent.

It is not hard to see where this goes. If program-space search keeps
compounding with model capability, harness design stops being artisanal:
you don't hand-write a scaffold any more than you hand-tune weights — you pick
an optimizer, point it at your agent, and pay for the lift. Agent optimization
becomes a component you choose the way you choose Adam over SGD. For that
future to arrive, one question has to have a measurable answer: *which of these
methods actually works, on what, and at what cost?*

Right now it doesn't. Every optimizer paper grades its own homework: its own
tasks, its own seed agents, its own budget, its own base model — and, when
baselines appear at all, its own reimplementation of the competition. The
numbers never meet. A field that cannot compare its methods cannot tell whether
it is making progress.

![What comparison under one protocol looks like — an early sweep of sixteen
optimizers on BBH-hard, same seed agent, same budget meter. Ranks reorder as
budget grows; a leaderboard is just the right-hand edge of this
plot.](figures/anytime_curve_bbh.png){#fig-anytime-bbh width=95%}

MABench is our attempt at the measuring stick. It runs agent-optimization
methods — vendored verbatim, never reimplemented — against the same seed
agents, on the same task suites, under the same metered budget, with test
scores sealed until the run is over. The method is the only variable. The
deliverable is not a leaderboard number but an anytime curve — how much lift
over the seed agent a method buys per dollar spent — reported across a grid of
tasks, seeds, and budgets. This post explains the protocol: what a run is, what
gets measured, and why we made the design choices we did. Part 2 reports what
happened when we ran it.

## The unit of evaluation is a process, not a model

- Why the standard benchmark playbook breaks here: you're not scoring an
  artifact, you're scoring a *procedure* that spends money to produce artifacts.
- Consequence 1: the metric is **Δ over seed**, not absolute score. A method
  that "achieves 65%" tells you nothing until you know the seed scored 61%.
- Consequence 2: cost is not an implementation detail, it's an axis. The
  deliverable is an **anytime curve** — sealed test score as a function of
  dollars spent — not a number.
- Consequence 3: every result is conditional on (task × seed × budget × model).
  We report the grid; we do not marginalize it into a leaderboard. Say why,
  plainly, and take the flak for it here rather than in reviews.

## One run, mechanically

- Walk one run end to end, second person or narrated: method gets a workspace,
  a seed agent, and a budget. It can do anything in the workspace.
- The three metered endpoints and what each discloses — the **disclosure
  ladder**: `run_train` returns full trajectories, `score_dev` returns a
  scalar, `score_test` is sealed until the run ends. Spend is free to query.
- Two-facet feedback: the dataset's verdict *and* the worker's trajectory.
  Why methods need both (GEPA reads trajectories; hill-climbers only need
  scalars).
- **Stamps**: every time the method says "this is my best so far," we record
  (spend, candidate). That sequence *is* the anytime curve. The method never
  grades itself.
- Per-actor ledger: meta-spend (the optimizer thinking) vs. worker-spend (the
  agent doing tasks) metered separately. Real asymmetry to preview: one method
  burns \$150/run mostly on meta; another spends almost everything on workers.

## Faithfulness, or: don't rewrite the methods you're judging

- The failure mode of every methods-comparison paper: reimplement competitors,
  reimplement them badly, win.
- Our rule: methods are **vendored verbatim** behind thin adapters. The method
  owns its search loop; the framework owns identity, scoring, budget, metering.
  We do not invert control, we do not port, we do not "fix."
- The cost of that rule: methods keep their native selection logic, native
  hyperparameters, native prompts — so some differences between methods are
  differences in *tuning effort by their authors*. Name this honestly.

## The grid

- Carriers: GPQA (one-shot QA), CharXiv (one-shot), τ²-bench and
  terminal-bench (launchable agents). Why both forms matter — some methods
  can't even *express* an edit to a launchable agent. [small table]
- Seeds: five per carrier, spanning an abstraction axis from bare prompt to
  full agent scaffold. A method that lifts a weak seed may do nothing to a
  strong one — that's a finding, not noise.
- Methods, placed on the **coupling × surface** grid: what the method may
  touch (prompt / workflow / source) × how tightly it couples to the task.
  GEPA · AFlow · AdaEvolve · Meta-Harness · a coding agent · HGM ·
  prompt-hill. [the grid figure]

## What can go wrong (and what we did about it)

- Reward hacking the harness: methods run LLM-authored code — the sealed test
  set and the metering must survive an adversary. The syscall jail; what it
  covers today and what it doesn't. Be specific about the gap.
- Dev→test overfitting: methods select on dev; we report sealed test. Preview
  Part 2: the gap is real and method-dependent.
- Floor noise & nondeterminism: 5 seeds, multiple replicates, and even then —
  the null baseline's variance is the noise floor every claimed lift must clear.
- The one we can't engineer away: construct validity. Is "good at optimizing
  agents" one ability, or is every cell of the grid its own skill? We don't
  know yet. Say so.

## Where this sits

- Lineage: NAS-Bench, HPOBench — benchmarks *of optimizers*, where the search
  method is the subject and the objective is fixed. Not a gym (nothing is
  being trained), not an agent leaderboard (agents are held fixed).
- Close with the pointer to Part 2: what actually happened when we ran the
  grid on GPQA — including the method that spent \$100 to lose to \$0.82.
